* Move the published site into site/

The cloudflare-site pack publishes exactly one directory — assets.directory in
a wrangler.json — and its publishes-a-site-directory check blocks pointing that
at the repo root, which here holds the vendored mount, the queue workers,
scraper/ and ~10 MB of pipeline inputs. Its release task has no build step: it
uploads the committed tree verbatim. So the published tree has to exist in the
repo as a directory before the host can change.

This is that reshape and nothing else. GitHub Pages still publishes, at the same
URLs: publish_root=site makes site/ the artifact's root, so "/" is still the Now
page and no fetch path in any page moves — every one of them was already
page-relative.

The split is now structural rather than a list of exclusions. data/ keeps the
pipeline's own working files (the master, the price cache, the raw caches);
site/data/ holds the wire files the browser fetches, so site.config can name
`data` as a plain directory where it used to enumerate six paths to hold back
the two 10 MB inputs. normalize.py names the two roots, and the workflows and
task workers that commit generated data stage both.

package.json cannot ride along: it is the repo's npm manifest at the root,
outside the published tree, and a tracked copy inside it would be a version free
to drift. The pages read site/version.json instead — the one fact they wanted out
of it — and both records are named in version_files, so the bump rewrites them
together and refuses outright unless they already agree.

Proved by the goldens: all 110 UI requirement cases pass pixel-identical, and the
served tree was driven in a real browser — all three pages fetch /version.json
and show the committed version, with no application console errors.

Closes #730

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UaraYPNCgTxmYNDqNEk1sD

* Cover the published half of the data-dir check

The move gave edfringe-data-dir-is-generator-output a second root to scan, and
left every negative fixture in its suite under data/ — including the Jerusalem
lookalike, whose allowed counterpart had moved to site/data/. Deleting
'site/data/' from DATA_ROOTS entirely kept the whole suite green, so the half
that is actually served to visitors was unguarded.

Repairs the Jerusalem pair so the lookalike sits beside the file it looks like,
and adds a case for a hand-made file under the published tree. Both go red on
that mutation and green with the root restored.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_019hju6CLU4CHGbjffqMV6MN

* Scrape the Jerusalem Comedy Festival programme into data/jerusalem/

One-shot: the festival has no availability feed, no prices and no
cancellations, so there is nothing for a scheduled task to refresh.

The WP REST API gives identity (34 shows, 47 performances, 6 venues, their
categories); dates, start times, ticket links, addresses and running times are
only in each event's rendered page, so parse.py reads them out of that markup.
Hebrew end to end, and its self-test is the offline gate on a parsing change —
the fetch half can only be checked against the live site.

Venue performance counts reproduce the eventlocation taxonomy's own counts
exactly, which is the source's own end-to-end check.

Refs #727

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_019hju6CLU4CHGbjffqMV6MN

* Make the shared planner pieces festival-agnostic

Three places named Edinburgh where they only needed to be told:

- stayLink takes its city, Booking.com edition and currency, so a second
  festival's bed link is the local site rather than an English page with a
  foreign query string; the Edinburgh defaults are unchanged.
- israelTravelLink / israelRailLink: Omio does not sell Israel, so the paid
  partner there is Kiwitaxi's airport transfers, with Israel Railways offered
  beside it and untagged by design — it runs no programme, and hiding it to
  protect a commission would make the planner worth less.
- toIcs takes a timezone, and carries that zone's own VTIMEZONE. Israel's DST
  starts on the Friday before the last Sunday in March, not the Sunday, so it
  needs rules of its own rather than a reused European block.
- eligibleSlots uses a catalogue-supplied show URL where there is one, instead
  of deriving an edfringe.com URL from the slug.

Refs #727

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_019hju6CLU4CHGbjffqMV6MN

* Add the /planJerusalem festival planner page

The Fringe planner's board, grid and schedule, driven by a festival descriptor
(planJerusalem/festival.js) rather than by anything Jerusalem-specific. It
imports plan/plan.css whole and redefines its brand tokens, and it imports the
pure engine from plan/lib/ — so the UI is a clone rather than a fork, and a
third festival is a descriptor, a theme block and its own scraped catalogue.

It shares no state with the Fringe planner: every key it writes is under its
own storage prefix.

Where it deliberately differs, and why:
  - no favourites upload. This festival publishes no export, so the empty board
    browses the whole 34-show programme instead.
  - two grid colours, not seven. The source publishes no live availability and
    nothing is ever cancelled, so the Fringe palette would draw a distinction
    the data never makes.
  - no re-plan animation, no draggable schedule furniture. Both earn their code
    on 25 days and 4,000 shows; on five nights they are not what makes the page
    good.

Hebrew is marked as Hebrew everywhere a show, venue or category is rendered,
and Heebo is loaded in front of the site's own faces, which carry no Hebrew.

Refs #727

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_019hju6CLU4CHGbjffqMV6MN

* Prove the Jerusalem planner: cases and goldens for 18.1-18.9

Five screen goldens (chrome, the empty board, one Hebrew show as both a lane
and a search row, the day grid, the schedule), three behavior cases (the bed
link's URL, the two transport links, starred shows surviving a reload without
touching the Fringe planner's keys) and one logic case (Asia/Jerusalem ICS, and
a show with no published running time exporting as an instant). The coverage
gate is green again.

Two harness additions the goldens needed:

- Heebo is vendored into the font jail. Inter and Plus Jakarta Sans carry no
  Hebrew at all, so without it every show name in a golden would have been a
  row of tofu boxes — a record of the renderer's font set rather than of the
  product, which is exactly what the jail exists to prevent.
- the fixture dataset gains data/jerusalem/shows.json, copied verbatim with no
  cast and no ADJUST: the whole festival is smaller than any selection worth
  making, and Part V asserts the real programme. No existing fixture is
  re-cast, so no committed golden moves.

edfringe-data-dir-is-generator-output learns that data/ now has a second
generator: the Jerusalem output and its git-ignored page cache are named
alongside normalize.py's, by file rather than by directory, so a third festival
is still the moment a person confirms what is in it.

Refs #727

Three files this branch edited are scoped to a skill the session had not

input.title: Switch the site from GitHub Pages to Cloudflare (step 2 of the migration)
input.body:
The owner's ask, once #731 had landed: *"lgtm; release a new version; check the new version in the live site. In parallel you can add the cloudflare pack and start making the changes, create the human actions issue, and make the switch."*

Step 1 (#730 / #731) moved the published site into `site/`, which is what the `cloudflare-site`
pack's single-published-directory rule requires. This is the swap itself.

## What this does

Adopts the `cloudflare-site` canon pack through the install runner and undeclares
`static-website`. The two cannot both hold: `static-website` says the version moves with the
change and a push to `main` releases, while `cloudflare-site` has its nightly `site-release`
task cut the version itself and upload the tree. `sw/version-bumped` would demand a per-PR bump
the new model does not want.

Adds a root `wrangler.json` naming `site` as `assets.directory` and claiming `edfringenow.com`
and `www.edfringenow.com` as custom domains, pins a `compatibility_date`, and retires the five
`static-site-*` workflows, `.github/site.config` and the three composite actions that only the
Pages pipeline read.

Two things the pack's model changes about the product, both consequences of the release having
no build step:

- **The version stamp.** `bump-version.mjs` generates `title="version …"` into the published
  pages from `package.json`, and `version-stamp-matches-package` blocks a drifted one. The
  `site/version.json` that #731 introduced is replaced by that stamp, and the three pages read
  it out of their own markup rather than fetching a file.
- **The analytics beacon.** `scripts/build-site.sh` currently injects
  `CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` at build time; the release worker now does the substitution into
  the copy it uploads. The committed file keeps the placeholder either way, so
  `beacon-token-is-not-committed` stays green.

## The gap this opens

No canon pack owns generic CI. Undeclaring `static-website` removes `static-site-ci.yml`, which
is what runs `verify` and the conformance sweep on every pull request. This change has to author
the repo's own replacement or the PR gate silently disappears.

## Not this issue

The Cloudflare account itself — the zone, the registrar's nameservers, and the two repository
secrets — is filed separately as a handover issue, because only a person can do it. Until those
are done the release parks at `needs-human-action` naming what is missing, which is the intended
failure rather than a half-configured deploy.

The nameserver move is world-reaching: it affects every record on the domain, not just the site.

"id": "git-github",
"via": [
-      "id": "claudinite-lifecycle",
"id": "claudinite-tasks",
+      "id": "cloudflare-site",
"accept": [
+# Serving a site from Cloudflare
+- **Adding a file the site serves** — put it under the tree the wrangler config's
+  `assets.directory` names: that directory is the whole upload, so a file outside it is absent
+  from the live site with no error anywhere, and a file under it that is documentation rather
+  than page goes in `.assetsignore`.
+- **Writing a version number into a page** — don't: `title="version …"` is generated from
+  `package.json` by the pack's bump, and a hand-edited stamp names a build that was never
+  served. Repair a drifted one, consuming no version number, with
+  node .claudinite/shared/packs/cloudflare-site/bump-version.mjs --stamp-only
+- **Publishing the site from anywhere but the `site-release` task** — never: the task is what
+  cuts the version, gates on what has landed and parks where a person must act, and a second
+  publisher has none of that while its green run looks exactly like success.
+- **A release parked** — the lane is the diagnosis: `action` is a credential, a scope, the zone,
+  or a record the previous host left on a claimed hostname; `decision` is a surface the release
+  depends on changing underneath it; `failure` means read the trace. The
+  `releasing-a-cloudflare-site` skill says what each one wants.
+# cloudflare-site pack
+Active when a near-root `wrangler.json`/`.jsonc` declares `assets.directory` — a repo whose
+wrangler config describes a *site* rather than a Worker backend. It brings the nightly
+`site-release` task (cut the version, stamp the pages, push the bump, upload the tree, report
+what the domain answered), the version scheme itself, and the checks that keep the upload
+boundary, the version stamp, the beacon token and the single path to production honest.
+The Cloudflare account's own steps — the zone, the account id, the API token — are the pack's
+`adoptionHandover`, filed as a tracking issue when the pack is adopted. What a previous host
+left behind is **not** on that list: an inherited DNS record on a claimed hostname is resolved
+in public DNS by the release before it consumes a version number, and a workflow or `CNAME` file
+still publishing is a check's finding. A checklist of steps that are no-ops for most adopters
+teaches its reader to skim it.
+## Rules (`RULES.md`)
+| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
+| Only the published tree reaches the site | high | correctness | prose: <100 words |
+| The version stamp is generated, never typed | medium | correctness | prose: <50 words + check (`cloudflare-site/version-stamp-matches-package`) |
+| One path to production | high | correctness | prose: <50 words + check (`cloudflare-site/no-second-publisher`) |
+| What a parked release is asking for | medium | correctness | prose: <100 words |
+## Skills
+| Skill | Trigger |
+| [`releasing-a-cloudflare-site`](skills/releasing-a-cloudflare-site/SKILL.md) | any edit of a `wrangler.json`/`.jsonc` or the release task — held by the guard until loaded |
+## Checks
+| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
+| `cloudflare-site/publishes-a-site-directory` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
+| `cloudflare-site/version-stamp-matches-package` | medium | correctness | check: blocking |
+| `cloudflare-site/no-second-publisher` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
+| `cloudflare-site/beacon-token-is-not-committed` | high | legal | check: blocking |
+## Tasks
+| Task | Cadence | What it does |
+| [`site-release`](tasks/site-release/README.md) | daily, when the branch has moved past the last release | cuts the next version, stamps and pushes it, uploads the published tree to Cloudflare |
+## Upstream
+- Cloudflare Workers static assets and custom domains —
+  https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/ and
+  https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/routing/custom-domains/ (mirrored as
+  source at `raw.githubusercontent.com/cloudflare/cloudflare-docs`, `production` branch, under
+  `src/content/docs/workers/static-assets/` and
+  `src/content/docs/workers/configuration/routing/custom-domains.mdx`) — reconciled through
+- Wrangler releases — https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/releases (the same notes are the
+  `packages/wrangler/CHANGELOG.md` of that repository) — reconciled through `wrangler@4.131.2`.
+  The release pins `wrangler@4.128.0`; the pin moves in a commit that says so.
+<!-- A Claudinite pack badge. The colour and glyph below are this file's own — dev/tools/badges/render.mjs re-renders the template around them. -->
+<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 32 32" width="32" height="32" role="img" aria-label="Claudinite pack: cloudflare-site">
+  <title>cloudflare-site</title>
+  <defs>
+    <linearGradient id="b-cloudflare-site" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">
+      <stop offset="0" stop-color="#f6821f"/>
+      <stop offset="1" stop-color="#c06518"/>
+    </linearGradient>
+  </defs>
+  <rect width="32" height="32" rx="8" fill="url(#b-cloudflare-site)"/>
+  <path d="M9 20h13a5 5 0 0 0-7.5-7A7 7 0 0 0 9 20" fill="none" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2.2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"/>
+</svg>
+# Version history
+Records for `packs/cloudflare-site/pack.mjs`'s `version` field, one row per version, newest
+first. A version is cut on `main` after its changes land, so a row names the pull requests that
+landed between the previous version and this one; the weekly history task writes the rows a
+version is missing and leaves every row that already stands.
+| Version | Date | What changed |

+| 60913.1 | 2026-09-13 | The pack's first version: the `site-release` task, the version scheme and page stamp, the four checks, the `releasing-a-cloudflare-site` skill and the Cloudflare account's handover steps, generalized out of ClaudiniteWebsite's local pack (#1981). |

content.content:
1	---
2	name: releasing-a-cloudflare-site
3	description: How a site served from Cloudflare is released — the version contract, the guards that stop a release loop or a half-release, forcing one, rolling one back, and which parts of Cloudflare only a person can change. Use when changing the release task, the wrangler config or the analytics loader, and when a release parks.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
6	    - "**/wrangler.json"
7	    - "**/wrangler.jsonc"
8	    - "**/tasks/site-release/**"
9	---
10	
11	# Releasing a Cloudflare-served site
12	
13	A release is one thing: the default branch's tree, at a version the release itself cuts,
14	uploaded to Cloudflare. The `cloudflare-site/site-release` task owns all of it — its
15	[README](../../tasks/site-release/README.md) says what the worker does; this says how to
16	operate it and what a change to it must not break.
17	
18	## The four properties a change preserves
19	
20	- **The version names what shipped.** `package.json` is the only source and the page stamps
21	  are generated from it, so the bump and the upload are one run — and the bump goes first,
22	  because of the two possible drifts only one is invisible: a site serving a version the repo
23	  has no record of. A number consumed by an upload that then failed is visible in the park and
24	  costs nothing.
25	- **A release cannot re-arm itself.** The gate is "the branch has moved past the last release
26	  commit", read off the `Claudinite-Task:` trailer. Anything that makes the release's own commit
27	  look like ordinary work releases nightly, forever.
28	- **Only the published directory is published.** `assets.directory` is the outer boundary, and
29	  the repo around it holds the vendored mount, the queue's workers and the packs — none of which
30	  may reach a public URL. Inside it, `.assetsignore` holds back what is documentation rather
31	  than page, so a file landing there is not automatically a public URL.
32	- **The beacon token is injected, never committed.** A published loader ships with the
33	  placeholder and no-ops; the deploy substitutes the `CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` repository
34	  variable into the copy it uploads. Changing what the page loads or logs changes the promise,
35	  so the site's own privacy disclosure moves in the same commit.
36	
37	## Releasing now rather than tonight
38	
39	The release is the queue's, so force it the way any task is forced:
40	
41	```
42	gh workflow run claudinite-scheduler.yml -f wake=cloudflare-site/site-release
43	```
44	
45	The gate is still evaluated when the item is picked, so a force with nothing to release rolls
46	with its reason on record rather than shipping a duplicate.
47	
48	## Rolling back
49	
50	Revert on the branch and let the next release carry it — the revert sits above the last release
51	commit, so the gate opens on it; force the run with the command above when it cannot wait for
52	the nightly anchor. Don't add a rollback lever: it would be a second path to production, with
53	its own version arithmetic to keep in step.
54	
55	## What only a person can change
56	
57	Everything on the Cloudflare side — the account, the API token and its scopes, and whether the
58	domain is a zone on that account at all. The wrangler config claims the apex (and usually
59	`www`) as custom domains, so a deploy fails outright until the zone is there. That is the
60	intended failure: a release that quietly published to a URL nobody visits is worse than one that
61	stops and says so. Those steps are the pack's `adoptionHandover`, filed as an issue when the
62	pack is adopted.
63	
64	## What the previous host left behind
65	
66	Adding a zone imports the records the old host was serving, and a custom domain cannot be
67	attached over an existing `CNAME` — so an inherited `www` record blocks the deploy, and old
68	apex records keep serving the old host until they go. Nobody is asked to check for these: the
69	release resolves each claimed hostname in public DNS before it consumes a version number and
70	parks naming the record it found ([preflight.mjs](../../tasks/site-release/preflight.mjs)), and
71	`no-second-publisher` catches the repo-side leftovers — a workflow that still deploys, a `CNAME`
72	file still claiming the domain for GitHub Pages. An unreachable resolver is inconclusive, not a
73	verdict: the release proceeds and says the probe did not run.
74	
75	## Reading a park
76	
77	The worker names the lane it wants, so the label is the diagnosis. **`action`** is a credential,
78	a scope, the zone, or an inherited record, and the comment names which — nothing is wrong with
79	the code. **`decision`** means a surface the release depends on changed underneath it (no
80	`package.json` on the branch, no `assets.directory`, the analytics placeholder gone), and
81	whether the release should follow is a person's call. **`failure`** means read the trace; that
82	lane also holds the next occurrence until the item is woken or closed, so a broken release stops
83	rather than filing a queue of items that break the same way. A park after the push but before
84	the upload has consumed a version number — re-queue the item, and the retry counts from the
85	branch's new tip.
86	
87	## Changing the release
88

---
name: releasing-a-cloudflare-site
description: How a site served from Cloudflare is released — the version contract, the guards that stop a release loop or a half-release, forcing one, rolling one back, and which parts of Cloudflare only a person can change. Use when changing the release task, the wrangler config or the analytics loader, and when a release parks.
metadata:
  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
    - "**/wrangler.json"
    - "**/wrangler.jsonc"
    - "**/tasks/site-release/**"
---

# Releasing a Cloudflare-served site

A release is one thing: the default branch's tree, at a version the release itself cuts,
uploaded to Cloudflare. The `cloudflare-site/site-release` task owns all of it — its
[README](../../tasks/site-release/README.md) says what the worker does; this says how to
operate it and what a change to it must not break.

## The four properties a change preserves

- **The version names what shipped.** `package.json` is the only source and the page stamps
  are generated from it, so the bump and the upload are one run — and the bump goes first,
  because of the two possible drifts only one is invisible: a site serving a version the repo
  has no record of. A number consumed by an upload that then failed is visible in the park and
  costs nothing.
- **A release cannot re-arm itself.** The gate is "the branch has moved past the last release
  commit", read off the `Claudinite-Task:` trailer. Anything that makes the release's own commit
  look like ordinary work releases nightly, forever.
- **Only the published directory is published.** `assets.directory` is the outer boundary, and
  the repo around it holds the vendored mount, the queue's workers and the packs — none of which
  may reach a public URL. Inside it, `.assetsignore` holds back what is documentation rather
  than page, so a file landing there is not automatically a public URL.
- **The beacon token is injected, never committed.** A published loader ships with the
  placeholder and no-ops; the deploy substitutes the `CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` repository
  variable into the copy it uploads. Changing what the page loads or logs changes the promise,
  so the site's own privacy disclosure moves in the same commit.

## Releasing now rather than tonight

The release is the queue's, so force it the way any task is forced:

```
gh workflow run claudinite-scheduler.yml -f wake=cloudflare-site/site-release
```

The gate is still evaluated when the item is picked, so a force with nothing to release rolls
with its reason on record rather than shipping a duplicate.

## Rolling back

Revert on the branch and let the next release carry it — the revert sits above the last release
commit, so the gate opens on it; force the run with the command above when it cannot wait for
the nightly anchor. Don't add a rollback lever: it would be a second path to production, with
its own version arithmetic to keep in step.

## What only a person can change

Everything on the Cloudflare side — the account, the API token and its scopes, and whether the
domain is a zone on that account at all. The wrangler config claims the apex (and usually
`www`) as custom domains, so a deploy fails outright until the zone is there. That is the
intended failure: a release that quietly published to a URL nobody visits is worse than one that
stops and says so. Those steps are the pack's `adoptionHandover`, filed as an issue when the
pack is adopted.

## What the previous host left behind

Adding a zone imports the records the old host was serving, and a custom domain cannot be
attached over an existing `CNAME` — so an inherited `www` record blocks the deploy, and old
apex records keep serving the old host until they go. Nobody is asked to check for these: the
release resolves each claimed hostname in public DNS before it consumes a version number and
parks naming the record it found ([preflight.mjs](../../tasks/site-release/preflight.mjs)), and
`no-second-publisher` catches the repo-side leftovers — a workflow that still deploys, a `CNAME`
file still claiming the domain for GitHub Pages. An unreachable resolver is inconclusive, not a
verdict: the release proceeds and says the probe did not run.

## Reading a park

The worker names the lane it wants, so the label is the diagnosis. **`action`** is a credential,
a scope, the zone, or an inherited record, and the comment names which — nothing is wrong with
the code. **`decision`** means a surface the release depends on changed underneath it (no
`package.json` on the branch, no `assets.directory`, the analytics placeholder gone), and
whether the release should follow is a person's call. **`failure`** means read the trace; that
lane also holds the next occurrence until the item is woken or closed, so a broken release stops
rather than filing a queue of items that break the same way. A park after the push but before
the upload has consumed a version number — re-queue the item, and the retry counts from the
branch's new tip.

## Changing the release

- **Never add a workflow that publishes.** The release lives in code-work precisely because
  `wrangler` is a CLI and needs no `uses:` step; a workflow beside it would bypass both the
  version bump and the queue's failure lane. `no-second-publisher` refuses one, so don't also
  guard it in review.
- **Keep `wrangler` pinned to an exact version**, so two nights cannot run different toolchains
  without a commit saying so.
- **Correct the task README and this file in the same commit** as any behaviour change — a
  description that still says the old thing is worse than none.

+{
+  // What Cloudflare serves, and from where. The cloudflare-site pack's
+  // site-release task reads this file to learn both, and its checks hold the
+  // two answers honest.
+  "name": "edfringenow",
+
+  // Pinned, so the runtime a release lands on is a value in the repo rather
+  // than whatever the deploy day defaults to. Moving it is a deliberate commit.
+  "compatibility_date": "2026-09-16",
+
+  // There is no Worker script: this is a static site, so the whole deployment
+  // is the asset tree and `main` is deliberately absent.
+  "assets": {
+    // The ONE published directory, and the whole upload. A file outside it is
+    // absent from the live site with no error anywhere — which is why the
+    // scraper, the pipeline's working data, the vendored mount and the queue
+    // workers live outside it rather than being excluded by name. What is
+    // inside it but still not a page is held back by .assetsignore.
+    "directory": "./site",
+
+    // The default, stated: `/plan/` resolves to plan/index.html with the
+    // trailing slash, and `/privacy.html` is served without one — the URLs the
+    // site already had. Spelling it out is what makes a future change to this
+    // key a visible decision rather than a silent one.
+    "html_handling": "auto-trailing-slash",
+
+    // Serve site/404.html for a path matching no asset. The default is a bare,
+    // body-less 404, which would be a regression: Pages answered an unknown
+    // path with a real page. NOT "single-page-application" — this site is four
+    // pages and three planners, and answering every unknown path with
+    // index.html would serve the Now page under any URL a visitor mistyped.
+    "not_found_handling": "404-page"
+  },
+
+  // The hostnames a visitor types. Cloudflare writes each one's DNS record as
+  // the deploy attaches it, so no record is created by hand — but a record the
+  // PREVIOUS host left on one of these names blocks the attach, which the
+  // release's preflight resolves and parks on before consuming a version.
+  "routes": [
+    { "pattern": "edfringenow.com", "custom_domain": true },
+    { "pattern": "www.edfringenow.com", "custom_domain": true }
+  ],
+
+  // Off, because it defaults to ON: left alone it would publish this same site
+  // a second time at edfringenow.<account>.workers.dev — a public URL nobody
+  // chose, serving the product's pages under a name that is not the product's.
+  // Preview URLs take their default from this key, so they are off with it.
+  "workers_dev": false

gitDiff.patch:
@@ -0,0 +1,30 @@
+/* The released version, read out of the page's own markup.
+ *
+ * Every page that shows a version carries `title="version <n>"` on its footer
+ * line. That attribute is GENERATED — the release bumps package.json and stamps
+ * each published page from it in the same run, and a check fails the build if
+ * the two ever disagree. So the page already knows its version by the time it
+ * loads, and no page fetches a file to find out.
+ *
+ * All three front-ends need exactly this, which is why it lives here rather
+ * than three times over.
+ */
+
+/* Read the stamp, and take the attribute with it.
+ *
+ * Removing it matters: `title` is painted by the browser, outside the page, and
+ * this site deliberately replaced that tooltip with a styled popup it can
+ * position, key-navigate and screenshot (see version-popup.js). Leaving the
+ * attribute in the live DOM would put the native tooltip back alongside the
+ * popup that replaced it. The committed markup keeps it — that is what the
+ * release stamps and the check reads — and the page drops it on load.
+ *
+ * Returns null when the page carries no stamp, which is every page that does
+ * not show a version; callers treat that as "nothing to show". */
+export function readVersionStamp(root = document) {
+  const el = root.querySelector('[title^="version "]');
+  if (!el) return null;
+  const version = el.getAttribute("title").slice("version ".length).trim();
+  el.removeAttribute("title");
+  return version || null;
+}

lines: -name: Assemble the published site
-description: >-
-  Builds the Pages artifact directory from the repo's EXPLICIT publish set —
-  `publish_paths` under `publish_root`, and nothing else. The artifact is
-  composed from a named list rather than "the repo minus the dirs we know to
-  hide": a subtractive rule publishes every file nobody thought to exclude (a
-  draft, a scratch note, an agent-tooling dir, a key), and it publishes each new
-  one silently the day it lands. An additive list can only ever publish what the
-  repo asked for, and its failure mode — a file that does not show up — is
-  visible on the site.
-  Two loud guards, because a Pages deploy has no other reviewer: a publish path
-  that does not exist fails the run (a rename that silently dropped a directory
-  from the site is exactly what the explicit list is for), and so does an
-  assembled site with no index.html at its root (a site whose "/" 404s is a
-  broken deploy, not a deploy).
-  Composite so it adds no reusable-workflow nesting level, and used by both the
-  Pages deploy and PR CI, so a PR proves its publish set assembles before it can
-  break the live site.
-inputs:
-  publish_root:
-    description: Directory the site is rooted at ("." = repo root)
-    required: true
-  publish_paths:
-    description: Space-separated publish set, relative to publish_root
-    required: true
-  dest:
-    description: Directory to assemble into, relative to the workspace
-    required: false
-    default: _site
-outputs:
-  dest:
-    description: The assembled site directory (workspace-relative)
-    value: ${{ inputs.dest }}
-runs:
-  using: composite
-  steps:
-    - shell: bash
-      env:

-// .github/actions/, run by the release pipeline; dependency-free (node:

-//          "this is a new generation of the site" statement, and by this script

-//          changelog, a human) reads it as "later means bigger". The year digit

-//          previous release's n + 1 for every further release the SAME day.

-//          answers "how many times did we ship today", which is the only
-//          question it is asked.

-// absorbs it: the wrap bumps major, so 1.91231.4 -> 2.00101.1 and the ordering

-name: Read the site release config
-description: >-
-  Reads the repo's required `.github/site.config` (five explicit keys, no
-  defaults, plus the optional build_vars) and exposes them as step outputs, so
-  the vendored reusable workflows stay copy-verbatim and carry no repo values of their own. A missing file, a
-  missing or empty required key, or an unknown (typo'd) key fails the run —
-  never a silent fallback to a default publish set. Composite so it adds no
-  reusable-workflow nesting level, and dependency-free so it runs on a bare
-  runner.
-outputs:
-  publish_root:
-    description: The directory the published site is rooted at ("." = repo root)
-    value: ${{ steps.read.outputs.publish_root }}
-  publish_paths:
-    description: Space-separated publish set, relative to publish_root
-    value: ${{ steps.read.outputs.publish_paths }}
-  version_files:
-    description: Space-separated version records, first one the source of truth
-    value: ${{ steps.read.outputs.version_files }}
-  build_command:
-    description: The command producing the publish set ("" = nothing to build)
-    value: ${{ steps.read.outputs.build_command }}
-  test_command:
-    description: The repo's CI gate ("" = no tests)
-    value: ${{ steps.read.outputs.test_command }}
-  build_vars:
-    description: >-
-      Space-separated names of repo variables the build may read ("" = none, and
-      the only key a config may omit entirely). A caller that runs build_command
-      exports them first with the export-build-vars.mjs script beside this action.
-    value: ${{ steps.read.outputs.build_vars }}
-runs:
-  using: composite
-  steps:
-    - id: read
-      shell: bash
-      run: node "${{ github.action_path }}/read-config.mjs"
-#!/usr/bin/env node
-// Exports the repo variables a site.config declares in `build_vars` into the
-// build step's environment, via $GITHUB_ENV. Vendored beside read-config.mjs;
-// dependency-free (node: built-ins only) so it runs on a bare runner.
-// Two environment inputs, both set by the calling workflow:
-//   DECLARED_BUILD_VARS  the config's build_vars value (space-separated names)
-//   REPO_VARS_JSON       `toJSON(vars)` — the repo/org/environment VARIABLES
-// REPO_VARS_JSON is deliberately the `vars` context and never `secrets`: this
-// script's output feeds the step that produces the published artifact, and a
-// context that cannot carry a secret cannot leak one into a published page.
-// A DECLARED NAME WITH NO VALUE IS A HARD FAILURE. The alternative — exporting
-// an empty string — is the failure this whole config shape exists to prevent,
-// just one level down: the build succeeds, the page ships, and the feature that
-// needed the value is silently dead on the live site. Better to fail the deploy
-// with the variable's name than to publish a page with a blank token in it.
-import { appendFileSync } from 'node:fs';
-import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
-export function resolve(declaredText, repoVars) {
-  const names = (declaredText ?? '').split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
-  const resolved = [];
-  const missing = [];
-  for (const name of names) {
-    const value = repoVars?.[name];
-    // Unset and empty are the same failure: nothing usable behind the name.
-    if (value === undefined || value === null || value === '') missing.push(name);
-    else resolved.push([name, String(value)]);
-  return { resolved, missing };
-// $GITHUB_ENV is line-oriented, so a value containing a newline needs the
-// heredoc form; the delimiter is name-derived so it cannot collide with the
-// value's own text.
-export function toGithubEnv(pairs) {
-  return pairs
-    .map(([name, value]) => (value.includes('\n')
-      ? `${name}<<__EOF_${name}__\n${value}\n__EOF_${name}__`
-      : `${name}=${value}`))
-if (process.argv[1] === fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)) {
-  const declared = process.env.DECLARED_BUILD_VARS ?? '';
-  if (!declared.trim()) process.exit(0);
-  let repoVars;
-  try {
-    repoVars = JSON.parse(process.env.REPO_VARS_JSON || '{}');
-  } catch {
-    console.error('export-build-vars: REPO_VARS_JSON is not valid JSON — the workflow must pass ${{ toJSON(vars) }}.');
-    process.exit(1);
-  const { resolved, missing } = resolve(declared, repoVars);
-  if (missing.length) {
-    console.error(`export-build-vars: .github/site.config declares ${missing.length === 1 ? 'a build variable' : 'build variables'} with no value in this repo: ${missing.join(', ')}.`);
-    console.error('Set them under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables, or drop the name from build_vars.');
-    console.error('Failing here rather than building with a blank value, which would publish a page with the feature silently dead.');
-    process.exit(1);
-  if (process.env.GITHUB_ENV && resolved.length) {

-  // Names only — the values belong in the build's environment, not in a log.
-  console.log(`export-build-vars: exported ${resolved.map(([n]) => n).join(', ')}`);

name: CI

# The repo's own pull-request gate. This file is NOT vendored from a pack: the
# release pipeline that used to carry one moved to Cloudflare, where the release
# is a queue task rather than a workflow, and no canon pack owns generic CI. So
# this is ours to keep in step with scripts/verify.sh.
#
# It runs one thing, because scripts/verify.sh is one thing: the unit tests, the
# JS and Python parse checks, the normalizer self-tests, and the Claudinite
# conformance sweep — the same script the pre-commit hook runs, so passing
# locally and passing here mean the same.
#
# Deliberately NO `paths:` filter. A path-filtered conformance flow arms
# auto-merge and then never runs, leaving the repo's own maintenance PRs waiting
# forever (the basics `conformance-workflow` rule).
#
# What it deliberately does NOT do is deploy, or dry-run a deploy. The
# site-release task is the one path to production, and `no-second-publisher`
# refuses a `wrangler … deploy` line in any workflow — it cannot tell a dry run
# from a real one, and that is the right trade. The wrangler config is validated
# here anyway: `cloudflare-site/publishes-a-site-directory` runs inside the
# conformance sweep and fails on a config that names no published directory, a
# directory that holds nothing, or a missing compatibility date.
#
# The browser-driven golden lane is ui-requirements.yml, not this one, so this
# gate stays fast and browser-free.
#
# workflow_dispatch so a GITHUB_TOKEN-authored PR — whose opening GitHub never
# turns into a pull_request event — can still have this started on its branch.
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

jobs:
  ci:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          # The PR's real head, not the synthetic merge commit, so CI evaluates
          # what the session's own Stop hook evaluated.
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 22

      - name: Verify
        run: bash scripts/verify.sh

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/EdFringeNow/.claude/skills/writing-pack-prose

# Writing pack prose

Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.

**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.

## The ration

Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.

- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
  trigger.
- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs in the references doc
  below.
- **Moving a rule out of `RULES.md` into a skill** — only where the skill's
  `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` covers *every* moment the rule is needed. A skill whose only
  trigger is its description is picked by the model, not the harness, so a rule that must fire at
  a moment no file edit predicts stays prose, however activity-shaped it reads. (2)

## Shape a rule so it fires

- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
  reader to it.
- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
  to three neighbouring bullets.
- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
  you report the change.
- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
  it.
- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
  hand-built command. (1)
- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
  reader doesn't need at act time goes to the references doc below.
- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
  teaches a world the reader won't find.
- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.

## The references doc — where a rule's rationale lives

A pack keeps **one** `references.md` beside its `RULES.md`, servicing all of the pack's prose
files and its checks. It exists for maintenance and review — the periodic pass that asks
whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written — never for daily agentic
work: no rule sends its reader there, and no session loads it. So it stays in the repo that
owns the pack and never vendors: a member mounting a canon pack receives the rules, not the
reasoning behind them, and the pass that reaffirms them runs where the pack lives.

- **Adding a rule that has a rationale** — write the brief rule in `RULES.md` (or the skill),
  and put the reason in `references.md`. End the rule with the bare marker — `… never a
  filesystem walk. (3)` — and nothing else: don't name the references file, don't link it,
  don't ask the reader to follow anything. Not every rule needs one; a rule whose reason is
  self-evident from its consequence clause carries no marker.
- **Writing the entry** — one bullet per entry, keyed by the citing file's own namespace:
  `- **(RULES-3)** <reason>` for a rule in `RULES.md`, `- **(<skill-name>-3)** <reason>` for a
  line in that skill's `SKILL.md`; the marker in the prose file stays the bare `(3)` and
  resolves within its own file's namespace. Write the reason so a future review can **reaffirm
  the rule from it**: what would have to be true for the rule to be retired.
  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
    the error, the measured cost).
  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it.
- **Numbering** — numbers are stable identifiers, not positions: the next entry takes its
  file's next unused number, a removed entry leaves a gap, and nothing ever renumbers (a
  renumber breaks every marker at once). One entry may serve several rules in its file; a rule
  may cite several entries (`(3, 7)`).
- **A check's rationale** — the entry points at the check, since a declaration admits no
  comment and no new key: `- **(check:growth-write-scope)** <reason>`, same reaffirmation
  standard. There is no marker on the check side.
- **Removing a rule or check** — remove its entry in the same change, unless another rule
  still cites it.

The `references-integrity` check holds the mechanism together: every marker must resolve to an
entry in the pack's own `references.md`, and every `check:` entry must name a check the pack
still carries. The `rule-revalidation` task is the mechanism's consumer — it reaffirms
referenced rules and checks against their recorded reasons on its weekly pass.

## Migrating an existing pack onto the references doc

An existing pack — a repo's local pack, or a shared canon pack worked on canon-side (a member
never edits the mounted canon) — migrates opportunistically, one pack per pass, whenever a pass
is already editing it. An unmarked rule stays valid forever, so there is no fleet sweep to
force and no straggler to chase; the check only judges markers that exist.

1. **Create `references.md`** beside the pack's `RULES.md` on its first entry, not before.
2. **Work each rule**: keep the act-time consequence clause inline; move review-only rationale —
   the evidence story, inline issue ids, a cost the reader doesn't need mid-act — into an entry
   and end the rule with its marker. Shrink-only on the rules side: a rule may lose review-only
   rationale in this pass, never gain text.
3. **Recover the missing reasons from history, source-first**: for a rule that states no reason,
   read the commit that added it and that commit's PR and issue *before* re-reading the rule —
   derive the entry from the source, then diff against what the rule implied. The commit
   message, PR body and issue discussion are where this corpus already keeps a rule's evidence.
4. **Never invent an entry.** A rule whose reason can't be recovered stays unmarked — an audit
   or the `rule-revalidation` pass judges whether it still earns its place; a plausible-sounding
   fabricated rationale would let a future review reaffirm a rule on false grounds.
5. **Cover the checks** worth reaffirming with `check:` entries the same way, from their `why`
   text and their adding commit's PR.

## Evidence

The commit and its PR remain the archive — dates, session ids, quoted exchanges and the story
of the incident live there, never in the rule. What the references doc takes from them is only
the **reaffirmable core**: the reason and the minimum evidence a future review needs to re-test
it. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument — a cost the
reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.

input.title: Cloudflare account setup for the site deploy (human steps)
input.body:
Everything in the repo for the Cloudflare switch is done (#733). These are the parts that live on the Cloudflare account and at the registrar, which nothing in the repo can do.

- [ ] Add `edfringenow.com` as a zone — [Add a site](https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/:account/add-site)
- [ ] Point the registrar's nameservers at the two Cloudflare shows at the end of that flow
- [ ] Delete the inherited `www` CNAME and the four GitHub Pages `A` records for the apex — [DNS records](https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/:account/edfringenow.com/dns)
- [ ] Copy the **Account ID** — [Overview](https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/:account/workers), right-hand column, a 32-character hex string
- [ ] Save it as the repository secret `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` — [Actions secrets](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/settings/secrets/actions)
- [ ] Create an API token from the **Edit Cloudflare Workers** template — [API tokens](https://dash.cloudflare.com/profile/api-tokens), press *Create Token*, then *Use template* on that row; the value is shown once
- [ ] Save it as the repository secret `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` — [Actions secrets](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/settings/secrets/actions)

Done when `https://edfringenow.com/` serves the site and its response carries a `cf-cache-status` header instead of `server: GitHub.com`.

---

## What each step is for

**The zone and the nameservers.** `wrangler.jsonc` claims `edfringenow.com` and `www.edfringenow.com` as custom domains. Cloudflare can only attach a custom domain to a zone it hosts, so until the zone is Active and the nameservers point at it, every release parks at `needs-human-action` rather than deploying. That is the intended failure — a release that quietly published to a URL nobody visits is worse than one that stops and says so.

Moving the nameservers is the one step here that reaches beyond the site: it moves **every** record on the domain to Cloudflare, mail included. Cloudflare imports what it can see during the add-site flow, but check the imported list against the registrar's before you flip, because anything it missed stops resolving.

Everything in the repo for the Cloudflare switch is done (#733). These are the parts that live on the Cloudflare account and at the registrar, which nothing in the repo can do.

- [ ] Add `edfringenow.com` as a zone — [Add a site](https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/:account/add-site)
- [ ] Point the registrar's nameservers at the two Cloudflare shows at the end of that flow
- [ ] Delete the inherited `www` CNAME and the four GitHub Pages `A` records for the apex — [DNS records](https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/:account/edfringenow.com/dns)
- [ ] Copy the **Account ID** — [Overview](https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/:account/workers), right-hand column, a 32-character hex string
- [ ] Save it as the repository secret `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` — [Actions secrets](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/settings/secrets/actions)
- [ ] Create an API token from the **Edit Cloudflare Workers** template — [API tokens](https://dash.cloudflare.com/profile/api-tokens), press *Create Token*, then *Use template* on that row; the value is shown once
- [ ] Save it as the repository secret `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` — [Actions secrets](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/settings/secrets/actions)

Done when `https://edfringenow.com/` serves the site and its response carries a `cf-cache-status` header instead of `server: GitHub.com`.

---

## What each step is for

**The zone and the nameservers.** `wrangler.jsonc` claims `edfringenow.com` and `www.edfringenow.com` as custom domains. Cloudflare can only attach a custom domain to a zone it hosts, so until the zone is Active and the nameservers point at it, every release parks at `needs-human-action` rather than deploying. That is the intended failure — a release that quietly published to a URL nobody visits is worse than one that stops and says so.

**The two secrets.** The release stops at its own gate before it touches Cloudflare if either is missing, and parks naming which one — nothing is left half-done. A token narrower than the *Edit Cloudflare Workers* template instead fails inside wrangler with a `10000`-class error, which parks the same way but costs a round trip to diagnose.

```

npm run verify     # tests + JS parse-checks (node --check) + Python py_compile
```

`npm run verify` is the single gate: it runs the unit tests, syntax-checks every
JavaScript source under `site/`, and byte-compiles the `scraper/`
Python. The pull-request gate (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`)
runs it as the repo's `test_command` on every push to `main` and every pull
request, and a **pre-commit hook** runs the same gate
locally so nothing red is committed. Enable the hook once per clone:

```
npm run setup-hooks   # git config core.hooksPath .githooks
```

(Bypass a single commit with `git commit --no-verify`.)

## Development

Shared Claude working guidelines are vendored into this repo as committed files
via [Claudinite](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite) and refreshed by its
nightly maintenance — no session-time fetch. Session hooks and the
`Claudinite checks` CI workflow run the conformance sweep from the committed
snapshot, so every branch judges by the version it carries. How the vendored
mount works lives in the Claudinite repo (`mount/DESIGN.md`).

input.command:
git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Switch the site's host from GitHub Pages to Cloudflare

Adopts the cloudflare-site pack and undeclares static-website. The two cannot
both hold: static-website moves the version with the change and releases on push
to main, while cloudflare-site has its nightly site-release task cut the version
itself and upload the tree — so sw/version-bumped would demand a per-PR bump the
new model does not want.

wrangler.jsonc names site/ as the published tree and claims both hostnames as
custom domains. Two of its keys are set against Cloudflare's documented
defaults rather than left alone:

  - workers_dev defaults to TRUE, which would publish this same site a second
    time at edfringenow.<account>.workers.dev — a public URL nobody chose.
  - not_found_handling defaults to a bare, body-less 404. Pages answered an
    unknown path with a real page, so site/404.html keeps that promise; it is
    the one page whose URLs are root-relative, because Cloudflare serves it
    under whatever path the visitor actually asked for.

assets.directory uploads everything beneath it, which is wider than the Pages
publish set was: that list named plan/ file by file to keep the design mock out,
and could not exclude the __tests__ dirs it shipped. site/.assetsignore replaces
the enumeration and drops both — 113 files become 84. Its patterns were checked
against real gitignore semantics, which is what wrangler matches with.

The version moves onto the pack's generated stamp. There is no build step in the
release — it uploads the committed tree verbatim — so a published version.json
had nothing to write it. Each page now carries title="version <n>", stamped from
package.json by the pack's bump and guarded against drift by a check, and
shared/version.js reads it. The reader takes the attribute with it: title is
painted by the browser, and this site deliberately replaced that tooltip with a
styled popup it can position and screenshot. The harness pins the stamp, so the
goldens record the product rather than the day they were rendered.

Retires the five static-site-* workflows, site.config and the three composite
actions. scripts/build-site.sh goes with them: the beacon injection is the
release worker's now, and js/build-info.js was written by the deploy and read by
nothing. No canon pack owns generic CI, so ci.yml is the repo's own — it runs
scripts/verify.sh and nothing else, and deliberately does not dry-run wrangler,
which no-second-publisher refuses in any workflow.

Corrects what the switch falsifies. The caching comments said the host offered
no way to vary Cache-Control per file; Cloudflare does (_headers), but serves
assets must-revalidate with an ETag — so the client cache still earns its place,
for a different reason than the one written down.

Closes #733
Refs #734

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UaraYPNCgTxmYNDqNEk1sD
EOF
git log --oneline -1 && git show --stat HEAD | tail -6

input.title: Switch the site's host from GitHub Pages to Cloudflare
input.body:
Step 2 of the migration. #731 moved the site into `site/`; this swaps the host.

Closes #733

## The pack swap

Adopts `cloudflare-site` through the canon install runner and **undeclares `static-website`**. The two cannot both hold: `static-website` moves the version with the change and releases on push to `main`, while `cloudflare-site` has its nightly `site-release` task cut the version itself and upload the tree — so `sw/version-bumped` would demand a per-PR bump the new model does not want.

## Two config keys set against Cloudflare's defaults

Both verified against Cloudflare's own docs, not assumed:

- **`workers_dev` defaults to `true`** — left alone it would publish this same site a second time at `edfringenow.<account>.workers.dev`, a public URL nobody chose, serving the product under a name that is not the product's.
- **`not_found_handling` defaults to a bare, body-less 404.** Pages answered an unknown path with a real page (9,379 bytes, checked against the live site), so `site/404.html` keeps that promise. It is the one page whose URLs are **root-relative**: Cloudflare serves its bytes under whatever path the visitor actually asked for, so a page-relative `css/styles.css` would resolve against that unknown path and 404 in turn, leaving an unstyled error page.

Deliberately **not** `single-page-application` — this site is four pages plus three planners, and answering every unknown path with `index.html` would serve the Now page under any URL a visitor mistyped.

## The publish boundary got wider, so `.assetsignore` narrows it

`assets.directory` uploads *everything* beneath it. That is wider than the Pages publish set, which enumerated `plan/` file by file to keep the design mock out and could not exclude the `__tests__` dirs it knowingly shipped. `site/.assetsignore` replaces that enumeration: **113 files become 84.**

I verified the patterns rather than trusting the syntax — wrangler matches with the `ignore` npm package (gitignore semantics, and it auto-ignores `.assetsignore`, `_redirects` and `_headers` itself), so I tested the exact pattern set against real gitignore matching. All four `__tests__` dirs, the design mock and the two stray docs drop; no product file moves.

## The version moves onto the pack's stamp

The release has **no build step** — it uploads the committed tree verbatim — so the `site/version.json` that #731 introduced had nothing to write it. Each page now carries `title="version <n>"`, stamped from `package.json` by the pack's own bump and guarded against drift by a check; `site/shared/version.js` reads it.

The reader **takes the attribute with it**, because this repo deliberately moved the version *off* a native `title` tooltip — the browser paints those outside the page, so they can't be styled, keyboard-reached or screenshotted for the gallery (see `version-popup.js`). The stamp is a build-time carrier; the styled popup stays the UI.

The harness pins the stamp, so the goldens record the product rather than the day they were rendered — replacing the `version.json` fixture with one substitution that covers every page at once.

## What got retired

The five `static-site-*` workflows, `.github/site.config`, and the three composite actions. `scripts/build-site.sh` goes with them: the beacon injection is the release worker's job now, and `js/build-info.js` was written by the deploy and **read by nothing**.

No canon pack owns generic CI, so `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is the repo's own. It runs `scripts/verify.sh` and nothing else, and deliberately does **not** dry-run wrangler — `no-second-publisher` refuses a `wrangler … deploy` line in any workflow and cannot tell a dry run from a real one. The config is validated anyway, by `publishes-a-site-directory` inside the conformance sweep.

## A claim the switch falsified

The caching comments in `shared/data-cache.js` and `scraper/README.md` said the host offered no way to vary `Cache-Control` per file, which was the stated reason the freshness policy lives on the client. Cloudflare **does** (`_headers`) — but it serves assets `public, max-age=0, must-revalidate` with an ETag, so a browser re-checks every file on every load. The client cache still earns its place, for a different reason than the one written down, and both comments now say the true one. No caching behaviour changed.

## Verification

- `npm run verify` — 290 tests, no blocking conformance findings.
- `npm run test:ui` — **all 110 goldens pass pixel-identical**, so the version-stamp change moved no pixel.
- `wrangler@4.128.0 deploy --dry-run` parses the config and reads the tree.
- The served tree driven in a real browser: all three pages show `v1.60916.2` from the stamp with **zero** `version.json` requests, and no console errors.

## Blocked on you

#734 has the account steps — the zone, the nameservers, the two secrets. Until they are done every release parks at `needs-human-action` naming what is missing, which is the intended failure rather than a half-configured deploy. **The nameserver move affects every record on the domain, mail included**, not just the site.

## One decision left

The first Cloudflare release computes its version as `1.0916.N` — the pack's scheme is `<major>.<mmdd>.<n>`, four digits where `static-website` used five (`1.60916.2`). The patch counter stays monotonic so ordering still holds, but the middle number visibly shrinks. Raising the major at the switch (`2.0916.N`) would absorb that, and "a new generation of the site" is arguably what changing hosts is — but the major is yours to declare, so it is untouched here.

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.

- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.
